title: ROI, Residual Income, EVA & Surety Performance (CMA P1-C · feeds P2-A/BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — performance determines capacity

MBG context: a vehicle and equipment loan reconciliation covered 13 accounts and tied post-adjustment to $310,000.00. Sureties and lenders look beyond profit to working capital, leverage, backlog quality, cash, and reliable WIP estimates. A project can report margin while consuming liquidity; an entity can grow revenue while reducing bonding capacity.

Performance measures translate accounting data into decision signals. ROI, residual income, and economic value added evaluate returns relative to capital. Their usefulness depends on consistent definitions, correct entity boundaries, and adjustments for accounting choices.

Return on investment

ROI = Operating income ÷ Average operating assets

DuPont decomposition gives:

ROI = (Operating income ÷ Sales) × (Sales ÷ Average operating assets)

The first term is operating margin; the second is asset turnover. A manager can improve ROI through price/mix, cost control, asset utilization, working capital, or disposal of unproductive assets. Each action has risk: delaying necessary investment or rejecting good projects can increase current ROI while harming value.

Assume an illustrative division has $400,000 operating income, $4,000,000 sales, and $2,000,000 average operating assets. Margin is 10%, turnover 2.0, and ROI 20%. The decomposition ties: 10% × 2.0 = 20%.

Residual income

Residual income = Operating income − (Required rate × Average operating assets)

Using the illustrative division and a 12% required rate, capital charge is $240,000 and residual income is $160,000. Residual income encourages acceptance of projects earning above the required rate even if they reduce the division's percentage ROI.

Suppose a new illustrative project requires $500,000 and earns $80,000, a 16% return. It exceeds the 12% requirement and adds $20,000 residual income. Combined operating income becomes $480,000 and assets $2,500,000, so combined ROI falls from 20% to 19.2%. An ROI-only manager may reject a value-adding project; residual income aligns better with absolute value creation.

Residual income favors larger centers in absolute dollars, so compare trends and scale carefully. Required rates should reflect risk and capital policy rather than being changed to produce desired rankings.

Economic value added

EVA is a refined residual-income concept:

EVA = NOPAT − (WACC × Invested capital)

NOPAT is net operating profit after tax; invested capital is operating capital supplied by debt and equity; WACC is the weighted average cost of capital. EVA may adjust accounting measures to better approximate economic investment and performance, such as selected R&D, leases, or nonrecurring items, depending on the defined system.

Assume illustrative NOPAT of $500,000, invested capital $3,000,000, and WACC 10%. EVA is $200,000. Positive EVA means operating return exceeded the capital charge; it does not mean cash increased by $200,000.

Measurement choices

Define the numerator and denominator consistently. If operating income excludes interest, operating assets should exclude financing assets/liabilities as defined. Use average assets because income spans a period. Gross versus net book value changes ROI as assets age; net book value can make an unchanged operation appear to improve through depreciation alone.

Allocations and transfer prices affect segment income. Idle assets, construction WIP, goodwill, leases, and shared cash require policy. Do not compare MBG and Riverton using different definitions or combine their capital without a clear consolidated measure and eliminations.

Inflation, accounting estimates, and project timing can distort measures. Pair financial ratios with WIP quality, forecast accuracy, schedule, safety, customer, and control indicators.

Surety and bonding lens

Surety underwriting commonly considers character, capacity, and capital. Financial analysis may include working capital, net worth, leverage, profitability, cash flow, backlog, job schedule quality, under/overbillings, and loss history. Exact underwriting formulas and thresholds vary by surety; do not invent a universal “bonding capacity equals X times working capital” rule.

Basic measures include:

Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities

Debt-to-equity = Total debt ÷ Equity

Assume an illustrative entity has $3,000,000 current assets, $2,000,000 current liabilities, $1,500,000 debt, and $2,500,000 equity. Working capital is $1,000,000, current ratio 1.5, and debt-to-equity 0.6.

Classify assets realistically. Stale or unsupported WIP and uncollectible receivables weaken quality even when included in current assets. Overbilling may provide cash but represents future performance. Underbilling may be an asset but also signals financing of work or billing/collectibility risk.

Backlog and profit fade

Backlog is remaining contract value on awarded work under a defined policy. Gross backlog alone is not profit or cash. Analyze expected margin, duration, customer, geography, capacity, financing, and cancellation/change-order risk.

A backlog profit estimate should reconcile to job schedules. Gross-profit fade reduces expected future earnings and may signal weak estimating or execution. A surety values timely recognition of problems more than optimistic delay. The case discipline from MBG's exact-amount convention and WIP review supports credibility.

Case debt context and decisions

The fictionalized $310,000.00 post-adjustment vehicle/equipment loan total is a case portfolio balance, not an illustrative WACC input. Performance analysis should tie debt schedules to the GL, separate principal and interest, confirm collateral and maturities, and model cash service. Equipment may improve capacity and margin but consumes capital and can reduce liquidity.

When evaluating an equipment investment, measure incremental NOPAT, working capital, maintenance, tax effects, disposal value, and capital employed. Do not evaluate only the accounting depreciation or the debt payment.

Measure design and gaming risk

ROI can rise when a manager delays maintenance, reduces training, accelerates revenue, or disposes assets needed for future growth. Residual income can encourage scale but may still reward short-horizon accounting income. EVA attempts economic adjustments but becomes opaque if adjustments are numerous or discretionary. Use transparent definitions and multi-year trends.

Investment decisions should use incremental cash flows and risk-adjusted discount rates; accounting performance measures evaluate stewardship after or during investment. Do not approve a project solely because its first-year ROI is high or reject it solely because depreciation lowers accounting income.

Use beginning, ending, or average assets consistently. Average operating assets usually aligns a period's income with capital employed, but major mid-period acquisitions may require monthly weighting. Decide treatment of construction in progress, idle equipment, leased assets, accumulated depreciation, and allocated corporate assets before comparing centers.

Surety package controls

A defensible surety package reconciles trial balance, WIP schedule, backlog, receivables, under/overbillings, debt schedules, cash, and covenant calculations. Explain significant fade, loss jobs, aged underbillings, stale receivables, and intercompany balances. Do not improve ratios by netting unrelated accounts or moving obligations across entities.

Stress test backlog. Assume illustratively $10,000,000 backlog at 15% expected gross margin, or $1,500,000 profit. If estimated cost rises enough to reduce margin to 10%, expected profit falls to $1,000,000—a $500,000 fade. Model the liquidity needed to perform the remaining work and the timing of billings, not profit alone.

Qualitative credibility matters. Timely, exact, reconciled reporting can support confidence; unexplained changes and repeated late loss recognition weaken it. The goal is not to present the most favorable ratio but to demonstrate controlled capacity to complete obligations.

Worked example — EVA from the financial statements

The EVA formula is short; the work is in building invested capital and the capital charge. Take an illustrative MBG divisional balance sheet and income statement.

EBIT is $1,200,000 and the tax rate is 25%, so NOPAT is $1,200,000 × (1 − 0.25) = $900,000.

Total assets are $9,400,000. Non-interest-bearing current liabilities are accounts payable of $1,300,000 plus accrued expenses of $400,000, or $1,700,000. Invested capital is $9,400,000 − $1,700,000 = $7,700,000, financed by $3,080,000 of debt and $4,620,000 of equity — weights of 40% and 60%, which is confirmed by $3,080,000 ÷ $7,700,000 = 0.40.

With a pre-tax cost of debt of 8% and a cost of equity of 12%, the weighted average cost of capital is (0.40 × 8% × (1 − 0.25)) + (0.60 × 12%) = 2.4% + 7.2% = 9.6%. Note the tax shield: the after-tax cost of debt is 6%, not 8%.

The capital charge is $7,700,000 × 9.6% = $739,200, so EVA is $900,000 − $739,200 = $160,800. The division earned $160,800 more than the return its capital providers required. It did not generate $160,800 of cash; EVA is an economic-profit measure, not a cash measure.

Trap — charging capital on total assets

Trap: invested capital excludes non-interest-bearing current liabilities, because suppliers and accrued payroll do not demand a return. Applying the 9.6% charge to the full $9,400,000 of total assets gives $902,400 and an EVA of negative $2,400. The same division flips from value-creating to value-destroying on a definitional error of $1,700,000 in the denominator. Whichever convention an organization adopts, it must be applied consistently across periods and across every division being compared.

Worked example — where ROI and residual income disagree

Use the illustrative division with $400,000 of operating income, $2,000,000 of average operating assets, and a 12% required return. ROI is 20.0% and residual income is $400,000 − $240,000 = $160,000.

Case one — an acceptable project

A new project requires $500,000 of assets and earns $80,000, a 16% return. Combined income becomes $480,000 on $2,500,000 of assets, so ROI falls to 19.2%. Residual income rises to $480,000 − (12% × $2,500,000) = $480,000 − $300,000 = $180,000, an increase of exactly (16% − 12%) × $500,000 = $20,000. An ROI-measured manager rejects a project that adds $20,000 a year of value.

Case two — an acceptable activity the manager will drop

Now suppose part of the existing division earns 13%: $52,000 of income on $400,000 of assets. Shedding it leaves $348,000 of income on $1,600,000 of assets, so ROI rises from 20.0% to 21.75%. Residual income falls to $348,000 − $192,000 = $156,000, a loss of exactly (13% − 12%) × $400,000 = $4,000 per year. The metric rewards the manager for destroying value.

Trap — the ROI hurdle is the division's own ROI, not the cost of capital

Trap: a manager evaluated on ROI faces an implicit hurdle equal to the division's current ROI of 20%, not the organization's 12% required return. Every opportunity between 12% and 20% is accepted by the group and rejected by the division. The higher-performing the division, the worse the distortion — which is why residual income and EVA exist, and why an investment centre's incentive design has to state which measure governs capital decisions.

Worked example — how asset measurement moves the answer

The denominator convention can matter more than performance. Assume an illustrative $1,000,000 asset depreciated straight-line over ten years with no residual value, generating a constant $150,000 of operating income.

MeasureYear 1Year 5Year 9
Year-end net book value$900,000$500,000$100,000
ROI on net book value16.67%30.00%150.00%
ROI on gross book value15.00%15.00%15.00%

Operations never changed. Net-book-value ROI nearly tenfolds purely because accumulated depreciation shrinks the denominator, while gross-book-value ROI correctly reports a flat 15%.

Trap — the aging-asset incentive

Trap: a manager measured on net-book-value ROI is rewarded for not replacing equipment and is penalized for investing, since a new asset resets the denominator to full cost. Comparing a division with old assets against one with new assets on net book value compares depreciation schedules, not performance. Fix the definition before the comparison: choose gross or net, choose beginning, ending or average, decide the treatment of construction in progress, idle equipment, leased assets and allocated corporate assets — then apply it everywhere.

Worked example — debt classification and bonding capacity

Return to the illustrative entity with $3,000,000 of current assets and $2,000,000 of current liabilities: a current ratio of 1.50 and working capital of $1,000,000. It now borrows $600,000 of cash. The economics are identical either way; the presentation is not.

StructureCurrent assetsCurrent liabilitiesCurrent ratioWorking capital
Before$3,000,000$2,000,0001.50$1,000,000
Revolver, classified current$3,600,000$2,600,0001.38$1,000,000
Five-year term note, noncurrent$3,600,000$2,000,0001.80$1,600,000

The same $600,000 of cash produces a current ratio of 1.38 or 1.80 and working capital of $1,000,000 or $1,600,000 depending on the term of the borrowing. Because surety underwriting leans heavily on working capital and net worth, the choice between a revolver draw and a term facility is a bonding-capacity decision made by the treasurer, not a presentation detail settled by the accountant.

Trap — improving a ratio without improving the business

Trap: restructuring debt from current to noncurrent, netting unrelated balances, or moving an obligation to an affiliate can move a ratio without changing a single cash flow. Sureties test for exactly this, and a package that improves on presentation while backlog quality, fade history and aged underbillings deteriorate damages credibility more than a weak ratio honestly explained. Reconcile the surety schedules to the trial balance and disclose the classification judgment.

CMA Part 2 / BAR Crossover

Part 2 expands ratio analysis, cost of capital, value creation, and financing. BAR connects performance measures to analytical conclusions and forecast assumptions. Expect questions where ROI and residual income recommend different decisions.

Practice and recap

  1. Define operating income and assets consistently.
  2. Decompose ROI into margin and turnover.
  3. Use residual income to test projects against required return.
  4. Calculate EVA from NOPAT and a capital charge.
  5. Evaluate surety ratios with asset quality and WIP evidence.
  6. Connect backlog, debt, cash, and operating capacity.

Recap: ROI measures rate, residual income measures dollars above a required return, and EVA measures operating profit after an economic capital charge. Surety analysis adds liquidity, leverage, backlog, and reporting credibility.

quiz.title: ROI, Residual Income, EVA, and Surety

questions.q: Illustrative operating income is $400,000 and average operating assets $2,000,000. ROI is:
Margin is 10% and asset turnover 2.0. DuPont ROI is:
Income $400,000, assets $2,000,000, required rate 12%. Residual income is:
A project earns 16% when required return is 12%. It generally:
choices: Must be rejected if current ROI is 20%
questions.explain: Its return exceeds the required rate even if it lowers the center's existing ROI.

questions.q: NOPAT is $500,000, invested capital $3,000,000, WACC 10%. EVA is:
Current assets $3,000,000 and current liabilities $2,000,000. Current ratio is:
Which statement about surety analysis is correct?
choices: Asset quality, WIP, backlog, liquidity, and reporting credibility matter
questions.explain: Sureties use multiple quantitative and qualitative factors; no universal single formula applies.
